turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can! Let’s keep it really simple.

1. What we sell

a. Roses

These are the star of the garden: shrubs that come back every year and bloom through the season.
Many shapes and sizes: small, medium, big climbers for arches/trellises.
Good if you want lots of color and classic flowers.

b. Perennials (non-rose plants)

Plants like lavender, coneflower, hosta, hydrangea, etc.
They also come back every year.
Great for filling in around roses or creating mixed flower beds.

c. Bulbs

Things like tulips, daffodils, alliums, ranunculus.
You plant the bulb/tuber in the fall, they sleep in the soil, then bloom the next spring.
These are great for early color before roses and perennials really get going.

d. Soil amendments & fertilizers

Soil amendments (mint compost, worm castings, cow manure, living soil, bone meal): improve your soil’s structure and nutrients so plants grow better roots.
Fertilizers (Founders Fish Fertilizer, OmniMeal, Boost & Bloom): “food” to keep plants growing and blooming well.
2. How to choose, in plain language

When you’re starting out, think about 3 things:

Your sun

Full sun: 6+ hours of direct sun. Most roses and many perennials love this.
Partial shade: 4+ hours. Good for shade-tolerant perennials; some roses are okay with this.

Your climate (hardiness zone)

At the top of our site you can pick your zone. The site will then show plants that can actually survive your winters.

Your goal

Want a rose-focused garden? Start with 1–3 roses and maybe a couple of easy perennials.
Want spring color first? Add some bulbs (tulips/daffodils) for fall planting.
Want to improve what you already have? Soil amendments and a simple fertilizer schedule will help.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You really only need a few basics to start off on the right foot, without overbuying.

1. One good soil amendment
This just helps your planting hole be a nice, cozy place for roots.

Our Get Growing Bundle is a simple all-in-one option if you like a kit.
Or choose just mint compost to mix into your planting hole. It helps retain moisture and protects roots.

2. One beginner-friendly fertilizer
Skip granular fertilizer at planting; a gentle liquid is easiest your first year.

Our Founders Fish Fertilizer is designed for healthy first-year growth and can be used about every 4 weeks during the growing season.

3. A good spot and simple routine
No special gear needed, just:

Sun: Aim for at least 6 hours of direct sun if you can.
Soil: Not pure clay or pure sand; adding compost helps a lot.
Water: Deep watering 2–3 times a week rather than a little every day.
Mulch: A couple of inches of mulch (like compost or bark) around the base, but keep it a few inches away from the stem.
